query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In frictional wear of HEA protective coatings, the dominant wear resistance mechanism is provided by the in‐situ formation of a stable, adherent oxide (or spinel) tribo-film that forms under elevated temperatures and oxygen-rich conditions, reducing friction and material removal.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy-alloy protective coating (e.g., AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5) with a known microstructure obtained via powder metallurgy or sputtering, exhibiting a solid-solution structure prior to wear.
generation.intervention: Perform tribological wear tests under controlled atmosphere conditions by varying the oxygen partial pressure (i.e., comparing oxygen-rich versus inert/vacuum environments) while using real-time surface characterization (e.g., in-situ Raman spectroscopy or synchrotron X-ray diffraction) to monitor oxide film formation.
generation.conditions: Wear tests conducted at elevated temperatures (around 300°C) with controlled contact loads in environments that either promote or limit oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and stability of a friction-induced, spinel-type or related oxide tribo-film at the coating surface.
generation.mechanism: During wear at elevated temperatures, friction locally raises the temperature at the contact interface, promoting oxidation. In oxygen-rich conditions, a protective oxide layer forms that adheres to the HEA coating, reducing direct metal-to-metal contact, decreasing the coefficient of friction and wear rate by acting as a barrier. In oxygen-poor conditions, diminished tribo-oxide formation leads to higher wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under oxygen-rich conditions, the HEA coatings will exhibit a measurable and stable oxide tribo-film, resulting in lower wear rates and a reduced friction coefficient compared to tests in oxygen-depleted conditions.
generation.baseline: Under inert or oxygen-depleted atmospheres, limited oxide formation will yield higher wear rates and friction, evidencing less surface protection.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold in high-temperature, high-load tribological conditions where frictional heating is sufficient to induce oxidation. Its applicability at lower temperatures or in conditions where other mechanisms (e.g., solid solution hardening) dominate remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence suggests oxide film formation is beneficial, the extent to which this mechanism alone governs wear compared to other strengthening effects is not fully isolated, and quantification of in-situ film properties remains challenging.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct paired tribological wear tests on identical HEA coatings at around 300°C using a sliding wear device. One set of tests should be performed in an oxygen-rich atmosphere while the other set is conducted in an oxygen-depleted (inert or vacuum) environment. Simultaneously, use an in-situ characterization technique (such as Raman spectroscopy or synchrotron XRD) to monitor the formation and evolution of surface oxide layers during wear.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and composition (via in-situ spectroscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxygen-rich environment does not result in a significantly thicker, stable oxide tribo-film along with a corresponding reduction in wear rate and friction coefficient compared to the oxygen-depleted baseline, then the hypothesis that in-situ oxide formation dominates wear performance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . decision.trend: In 2019, a study on AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high-entropy alloy coatings consolidated via powder metallurgy highlighted how spinel-phase formation at high temperature reduced friction and wear under reciprocating conditions. In 2020, a nanocrystalline CuMoTaWV coating produced by DC magnetron sputtering demonstrated enhanced hardness and wear resistance in both room-temperature and 300 °C tribological tests. These efforts underscore a broader push toward tuning chemistry and microstructure (e.g., through secondary phases or refined grains) to improve HEA coatings for wear resistance, but they leave open questions about which specific mechanism—solid-solution, dispersion/precipitation, tribo-oxide formation, or dislocation structures—dominates under operating conditions.
decision.unsolved: It is not firmly established which fundamental mechanism primarily governs wear performance in high-entropy-alloy protective coatings. The interplay of oxide-tribofilm formation, solid-solution strengthening, and microstructure evolution under tribological stresses and elevated temperatures remains insufficiently understood.
decision.lever: Conduct tribological tests in controlled atmospheres (e.g., varying oxygen partial pressure) while performing real-time surface characterization (e.g., high-temperature in-situ Raman or synchrotron X-ray diffraction) to track oxide or tribo-layer formation.
decision.why: A key testable mechanistic hypothesis is that friction-generated oxide or spinel layers provide the dominant wear protection in HEA coatings by forming a stable and adherent tribo-film that limits further material removal. By directly monitoring oxide evolution in controlled environmental conditions, one can confirm whether wear performance correlates with the in-situ generation of these protective films. The expected observation, if correct, is a measurable reduction in wear rate and friction when sufficient oxygen is present to form the protective oxide. Prior work on AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 and CuMoTaWV coatings suggests such films develop at higher temperatures, improving wear resistance. Conversely, if tests under oxygen-rich conditions do not produce reduced wear, or if the film does not form or fails to protect, that outcome would falsify the hypothesis.
